newsitem.title: USA: Exchanges see threat from information providers.
newsitem.headline: Exchanges see threat from information providers.

text.p: Trading exchanges face a greater threat from big information providers branching out into the financial transactions arena than from any of the smaller firms rushing to provide trading over the Internet, an exchange official told a derivatives conference Thursday.

Exchanges like the Chicago Board of Trade, which are losing a growing slice of their business to the over-the- counter (OTC) market and electronic and Internet trading, also have to watch out for companies like Reuters Holdings Plc, Dow Jones & Co Inc and Bloomberg LP, a CBOT official said.

Frederick Grede, executive vice president of the CBOT, told the Futures Industry Association annual conference here that he worries most about large information providers with huge resources behind them.

"What does keep me up at night, from the Chicago Board of Trade perspective, is those companies that do have the financial resources in the electronic transaction environment," he said in a panel discussion.

"Instinet last year made $580 million for Reuters," he said. "Dow Jones just announced $650 million they're going to put into Telerate, and one of their objectives is to make Telerate more transactions-sensitive. Bloomberg is doing great with his interactive transactions dealing system."
A spokesman for Reuters had no comment on Grede's remarks. Bloomberg and Dow Jones officials were unavailable for comment.

Grede said the EBS Group, an electronic broking service set up by a consortium of banks led by Citicorp and currently carrying out spot foreign exchange transactions, has a network of 2,000 terminals worldwide.
EBS investors know who their counterparties are and can execute their trades and get the settlement back in a matter of seconds.
"That's the standard we will be looking at in the future as far as the competitive environment of the transaction services are concerned," he said.

The CBOT is clearly feeling the heat from the OTC and cash markets as well, Grede said. He said Treasury bond futures volume on the CBOT has dropped by 16 percent in the last two years while OTC derivatives and cash Treasuries have experienced an upsurge in volume.

Rick Kilcollin, president of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, said a major attraction of electronic trading was that it was much cheaper than floor trade. All new exchanges that have started since 1986 have been electronic, he added.
End users of exchanges on the panel said exchanges could survive the competitive onslaught as long as they played up their traditional strengths -- liquidity, efficiency, clearing and anonymity.

"We're looking for deep, liquid, ordered markets and efficiency of execution," Robert Easton, chairman of Commodities Corp Ltd, told the panel. He said his company needs to be able to execute trades of size without upsetting prices.

John Sievwright, co-chairman of Merrill Lynch Futures Inc, said an open-outcry market made it much easier to interpret market sentiment and find out what was driving a market. That, he said, was an essential part of trading.
